title: Brandon Colorado Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Brandon wells are typically 45 feet deep, with a median reported yield of 15 gpm. See costs, water levels, permits, and risks.
h1: Brandon Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Brandon means understanding the local well records before you rely on a driller's estimate. The records show mostly shallow wells in plains alluvium and sedimentary rock, but the data is uneven: 163 permits are on record, while 101 report a total depth, 25 report a pump yield, and 10 report a static water level.

That makes nearby records useful for planning, not a guarantee for one parcel. A site-specific bid still depends on the lot, access, casing and grout requirements, pump equipment, electrical work, and the intended use of the well.

sections.heading: Brandon wells are usually shallow, but the outliers matter
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Brandon is 45 feet. The middle half runs from 40 to 52 feet, and 95% of the depth records are under 100 feet. For a driller's bid, that points to a relatively short bore in the ordinary case rather than a deep-rock project.

There are exceptions. The deepest well on record is 1,340 feet, and 4% of wells are 600 feet or deeper. Another 1% falls between 100 and 300 feet. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 155 wells in that category; 3 are listed as alluvial and 3 as Dakota. Those differences can make a neighboring well only a rough guide.

sections.heading: Reported Brandon yields are generally workable
sections.html:
Among the 25 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 10.0 to 45.0 gallons per minute. In the available yield records, 64% report more than 15 gallons per minute and 36% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute, and none falls in the 1-to-5-gallon range. That is encouraging for ordinary household planning, but the sample is small compared with the total permit count. Ask for the actual well test, not just a verbal estimate. A domestic well also must stay within its permit terms; an exempt household-use well is not an unlimited irrigation source.

sections.heading: Water levels near Brandon are shallow in the records
sections.html:
The 10 reported static water levels have a median depth to water of 30 feet. The middle half runs from 18 to 43 feet. Those figures describe the water level when measured, not the depth of the well and not necessarily the available drawdown during pumping.

The permit history does not provide enough decade-by-decade static water-level observations to establish a reliable dropping or rising trend. Do not assume the water table is stable just because many wells are shallow. A driller or pump contractor can check the well's static and pumping levels, recovery, and equipment sizing. Seasonal conditions, nearby pumping, and the aquifer named on the permit all matter to the practical supply.

sections.heading: Brandon has a long permit history and a few repeat drillers
sections.html:
Permits appear across the decades, with the largest recorded group in the 1970s at 26. The record also includes 3 permits from the 1950s, 11 from the 1960s, 5 from the 1980s, 18 from the 1990s, 14 from the 2000s, and 10 each from the 2010s and 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

Kemp's Well Service, listed as Kemp, George, is the most active driller in these records with 25 wells. Eastwood Drilling, listed as Eastwood, Francis, and Hoffman, listed as Hoffman, Earl, each appear on 7. These names show local permit history, not an endorsement. Verify current licensing, insurance, references, and what is included in a written proposal.

sections.heading: A typical Brandon well costs less at shallow depth
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a drilling rate of $35-$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 45-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,600-$2,500. That is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $7,600-$14,500. A bid can move outside that range if the lot needs unusual access, deeper drilling, different casing or grout, more trenching, or difficult electrical work. Request separate line items for drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, testing, trenching, and connection to the house so competing bids can be compared.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic space, and building plans
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main warning in the reported sample, but incomplete records and the 1,340-foot outlier show why a dry-hole allowance and clear contract terms matter. Confirm the permit's allowed use before planning household, stock, or irrigation demand. The records classify use as domestic or household at 25%, stock at 45%, and irrigation at 39%.

Water quality deserves separate attention. There are 10 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles of Brandon. That does not prove a problem on a particular parcel, but it supports testing an existing well and checking available environmental information before closing. Lay out the well, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and house together; a shallow water table or poor separation can affect septic and foundation decisions.

sections.heading: Use nearby records before buying or building
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel's DWR permit, construction report, well test, and water-rights documents. Then compare neighboring records, especially around Sheridan Lake, which is 8 miles away, and the more distant areas of Eads, Wiley, Hartman, and Cheyenne Wells. Nearby records can reveal depth variation, aquifer names, old equipment, and whether the local history is mainly domestic, stock, or irrigation.

For a new build, have a licensed Colorado well contractor inspect access and propose a drilling location before site work begins. Confirm the permit and intended use, budget for the complete system rather than the hole alone, and test existing water for the contaminants relevant to the area. A well that looks favorable on paper still needs a pump test and a practical septic and building layout.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Brandon, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Brandon is 45 feet, and the middle half ranges from 40 to 52 feet. About 95% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. The range is not uniform: the deepest record is 1,340 feet, and 4% of wells are 600 feet or deeper. Check neighboring construction reports before assuming your lot will match the median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Brandon?
faq.a: The local model uses $35-$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 45-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $1,600-$2,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $7,600-$14,500. A written bid should identify access, casing, grout, testing, and all equipment separately.

faq.q: How much water do Brandon wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 25 Brandon-area wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with a middle-half range of 10.0 to 45.0 gallons per minute. The reported sample has no wells under 1 gallon per minute. Because only 25 wells report yield, ask to see the actual pump test before relying on a production estimate.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Brandon, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. There are 10 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles of Brandon, so an existing well should be tested before purchase and periodically afterward. Review the well construction and permit records, identify the aquifer, and use a qualified laboratory. Nearby environmental mapping does not prove contamination on your parcel.

faq.q: Can I build a house on a lot with a Brandon well?
faq.a: A well can support a home only if the permit allows the intended household use and the lot can fit the well, septic system, house, driveway, and any required replacement area. Brandon records include domestic, stock, and irrigation uses, so do not assume every permit is a household permit. Verify the DWR permit, water quality, pumping performance, and septic feasibility before closing.
